claims.claim: Public court records are increasingly accessed through government electronic systems and commercial databases.
PACER is the federal courts' electronic public-records system.
Commercial databases reorganize court-record material available from government systems and provide it to paying customers.
Providers of electronic court-record access present convenience as a promised benefit.
Institutional users can absorb court-record access fees more readily than other users.
People unable to absorb those fees ration their court-record searches because of cost.
The court records at issue are created and maintained by public authorities.
Court records document judicial interpretation of law, prosecutorial uses of power, and the resolution of civil disputes.
Court records include filings that never receive news coverage.
Access to court-record material supports institutional scrutiny, journalism, legal research, and informed public participation.
A public court-record system permits technical access but makes sustained use unaffordable for some users.
Court-record access fees can appear modest when assessed one page at a time.
Court-record access fees are often described as charges per page.
Serious court-record research rarely starts with a known document.
Serious court-record inquiry requires searching, reviewing false leads, tracing related cases, and checking later docket entries such as motions, orders, exhibits, and amended complaints.
Researchers generally cannot know which court-record research path is relevant before paying to inspect records along it.
Charging for page-level inspection generates revenue from uncertainty in court-record research and raises the cost of exploratory inquiry.
Court-record access costs burden different categories of users unevenly.
Large law firms and data vendors can spread court-record database subscription costs across many clients.
Independent journalists, local advocates, small nonprofits, self-represented litigants, and community residents often cannot spread court-record subscription costs across many clients.
Private court-record databases add value beyond access to the underlying records.
Private court-record databases offer improved indexing, alerts, citation tools, and bulk-analysis capabilities.
Those database capabilities can save researchers time, especially when working across hundreds of dockets.
Some public court-record systems are difficult to search or expensive to use.
Difficulty or expense in public court-record systems can make premium private products the practical gateway to legal records.
Access gaps other than government-imposed court-record charges would remain under the proposed free public baseline.
Court-record access raises concerns in addition to cost.
Court files can contain addresses, medical information, financial records, and allegations that are later disputed.
Wider access to court files can increase harm caused by careless republication.
Wider access to court files can increase harm caused by automated profiling.
Fee-based scarcity protects people through obscurity only against users who cannot afford access, while well-funded actors can obtain the information.
Fee-based court-record access excludes users who cannot afford it.
Administering public institutions requires financial investment.
Democratic governance usually requires public investment.
Private court-record research services can continue to provide useful services above a free public-access foundation.
